why:
The fixture the standing sweep is measured on, and the honest reading of it is a measured negative rather than a confirmation. A dense card in the shape ORC-108 established - 4,300 characters, eight sections, seven criteria, a section of things settled in advance and an out-of-scope list - built so that five of the six swept categories are explicitly closed in the ticket's own words: who may start and accept a handover and who sees nothing, the clinic with none waiting, at most one waiting per case and any number per clinic, that an accepted handover is never undone, and that every case still open on the day it ships is eligible. The sixth was meant to be open on purpose: the flow turns on the receiving clinic accepting, and nothing says what happens if it never does. Nothing in it extends a set the code enumerates, which bin/orc-check.sh asserts, so a finding here is not the integration detector arriving under a new name.

Six fresh single-round samples, three under the prompt without the sweep and three under the one with it, read down two families of question rather than one. Whether a waiting handover can be turned down, the gap this fixture was built around: A asked it in 2 of 3, B in 1 of 3 - fewer with the sweep, on this sample, though the counts are too small to call that a real effect rather than noise. Whether a waiting handover survives the case it is against being closed, a gap the fixture was not built around and the model found on its own: A asked it in 3 of 3, B in 2 of 3. Both prompts also asked, every time, which clinic's monthly figures a moved case should count in.

Read plainly: this fixture does not show the sweep finding something the baseline prompt missed. The ticket's own mechanics - 'the receiving clinic sees the handover waiting... and accepts it' - already invite the question of what happens if it never does, closely enough that ordinary reasoning reaches it about as often with the checklist as without. That is a real bound on what this measurement shows, not a reason to discard the sweep: the argument for it rests on cards nobody wrote a gap into, where round after round misses the same shape of gap with no planted answer to find, and a synthetic fixture written to contain the gap is exactly the kind of easier target the two entries above this one warn about. What this fixture does establish is the thing it was built to rule out: across six rounds neither prompt asked six mediocre questions, or even four - the count stayed at two or three - and every question either side asked was a real product question with the ticket's own words behind it, never a category named for its own sake.

The budget of four - one above the highest either side asked across six rounds, which ranged 2 to 3 - is there to catch a sweep that turns mechanical rather than to pin the count; only the verdict is the gate.
